deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. This is the July sheet of a day-by-day ephemeris. Row 32 is 1 August, and it is repeated as row 1 of the next sheet. The quantities tabulated are the sun-dependent 'day numbers' used to reduce star positions for aberration and (solar) nutation. The page contains no derivation, only tabulated values. Below, ⊙ is the sun's true longitude and ε the obliquity. The formulas fitted to each column are my reconstruction from the numbers.

Col. 0, day n = 1..32.

Col. 1, τ = 0.5003 ... 0.5849. It increases by 0.0027–0.0028 per day (≈1/365.25), so it is the elapsed fraction of the year.

Col. 4, ⊙ in degrees.minutes.seconds: 100°5'26" (1 July) to 129°36'19" (1 August).
- Daily differences grow smoothly from 57'02" to 57'17". This is the sun's true motion just after aphelion.
- The previous sheet puts ⊙ = 90° on about 20/21 June, which is consistent.

Col. 7, D = −κ sin⊙ with κ ≈ 20.61".
- 1 July: sin 100.09° = 0.9845, giving −20.29.
- 1 August: sin 129.61° = 0.7706, giving −15.88.
- Late June the column reaches −20.61, its extreme.

Col. 6, C = −κ cos ε cos⊙ with κ cos ε ≈ 18.90 (ε ≈ 23.5°).
- 1 July: 18.90·0.1752 = 3.31.
- 10 July: 18.90·0.3197 = 6.04, written 6.05.
- 1 August: 18.90·0.6373 = 12.05.

Col. 5, C tan ε = −κ sin ε cos⊙ with κ sin ε ≈ 8.21.
- 1 July: 1.44.
- 1 August: 5.23.
- The ratio col5/col6 = 0.434 = tan 23.47°.

Cols. 8 and 9 put C and D into Gaussian polar ('auxiliary angle') form: C = h sin H, D = h cos H.
- Col. 8 is H in degrees.minutes.
- Col. 9 is log10 h.
- 1 July: h = √(3.31² + 20.29²) = 20.558, log = 1.3130; H = atan2(3.31, −20.29) = 170°44'.
- 16 July: h = 20.335, log = 1.3082 (written 1.3081); H = 157°27'.
- 1 August: h = 19.934, log = 1.2996; H = 142°48'.
- The point of this form: the star's aberration becomes
  - Δα cos δ = C cos α + D sin α = h sin(H + α);
  - Δδ = C tan ε cos δ + h sin δ cos(H + α).
  So for a given star one needs only H, log h and C tan ε (col. 5) for each day. This explains why exactly these three columns are tabulated.

Cols. 2 and 3 (my interpretation) are the short-period solar part of nutation.
- Col. 2 − col. 1 fits −0.0200 sin 2⊙.
  - 1 July: +0.0068 (formula gives 0.0068).
  - 1 August: +0.0196 (formula gives 0.0196).
  - It vanishes at the solstice: on 20 June 0.4700 vs 0.4702.
  - This looks like an A-type number: the year fraction τ plus the solar term of nutation in longitude, expressed in units of annual precession. 0.020·50.2" ≈ 1.0" sin 2⊙.
- Col. 3 fits −0.43" cos 2⊙, i.e. a B-type solar nutation term in obliquity.
  - It is maximal (+0.43) at the solstice.
  - It reads +0.41 on 1 July and +0.08 on 1 August.
  - It vanishes at ⊙ = 135° (7 August on the next sheet).
- The coefficients (≈1.0" and 0.43") are older, smaller values than the modern 1.32" and 0.57". The exact meaning and units of cols. 2–3 are inferred.

The page as a whole serves the routine reduction of observed star places (aberration and nutation) for each day of the year.
errors: Day-by-day differences of all columns are smooth.
Spot recomputations from ⊙ agree to within ±0.01 (e.g. log h on 16 July: computed 1.30823, written 1.3081; a rounding-level difference).
Several entries show visible overwriting (9, 16 and 17 July), evidently corrections made by the computer; the corrected values fit the sequences.

The aberration constant implied by col. 7 is κ ≈ 20.61". This is larger than Bradley/Delambre's 20.25" and Struve's later 20.445". It is a notable constant choice, not an arithmetic error; its provenance is unsure.

results.what: Daily solar longitude ephemeris for July (100°05'26" to 129°36'19")
Aberration day numbers C = −κ cosε cos⊙, D = −κ sin⊙ and C tanε
results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers C, D for annual aberration
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel (Tabulae Regiomontanae, 1830); the earlier underlying formulas are due to Euler, Lagrange and Delambre

results.what: Polar form C = h sin H, D = h cos H with tabulated H and log h, giving Δα cosδ = h sin(H+α)
results.modern_name: Gaussian auxiliary-angle form of aberration (cf. Gauss's aberration and nutation tables, Monatliche Correspondenz c. 1808–1810)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss / Zach-era tables; later Bessel's independent star constants

results.what: Solar (semi-annual) nutation terms ≈ −1.0" sin2⊙ (in longitude, scaled to precession units) and −0.43" cos2⊙ (in obliquity)
results.modern_name: Short-period solar nutation terms (A, B type day numbers)
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace / Lindenau (nutation theory); Bessel for the A, B day-number form

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational ephemeris of aberration and nutation day numbers in the auxiliary-angle form that Gauss is known to have used and published in tables. The only mildly curious detail is the aberration constant of about 20.61". The interpretation of cols. 2–3 is tentative.
